title: Where Your Heat Goes
description: Five ways a body loses heat, why wet and wind kill, and catching hypothermia early
tryIt: Fill two identical bottles with warm tap water, wrap one in a dry sock and one in a wet sock, and feel which has cooled more after half an hour.

concepts.title: How it works: five ways out
concepts.contentHtml:
It is only 8 degrees, but it has rained all afternoon, your jacket gave up an hour ago and the wind is finding every gap. You are not freezing. You are still in real danger, and the reason is physics.

Your core runs at about 37°C, and your body is always leaking heat to anything colder. The leaks have names. A review in the BMJ lists four: radiation, heat lost to surrounding cooler objects as infrared; conduction, heat lost to objects close to the skin, such as a chair, a bed or the floor;1 convection, the removal of body heat by air currents; and evaporation of water from the body. British Columbia's health service adds a fifth, respiration: every breath of cold air you warm and moisten carries heat away when you breathe out, and heat loss through evaporation and respiration rises in dry, windy weather.2

Water makes almost every leak worse. The same health service warns that wet clothing greatly increases heat loss through conduction and evaporation,3 and a standard physics table shows why: water conducts heat about 25 times better than still air (0.6 against 0.024 watts per metre per kelvin). Wind, meanwhile, strips away the thin layer of air your skin has warmed. That is what the US National Weather Service's wind chill describes: the rate of heat loss from exposed skin caused by wind and cold.4

The idea was born in Antarctica. In 1939–1941, on the US Antarctic Service Expedition, Paul Siple and Charles Passel ran experiments on temperature, wind and the time it took to freeze water in a test tube.5 On 8 May 1940 Passel's diary records an "excellent day for our experiment": in a blizzard with a wind of about thirty miles an hour, a cube holding 800 grams of water reached zero in about thirteen minutes,6 and his own nose began to hurt within thirty seconds.

concepts.title: In the field: catching the cold early
concepts.contentHtml:
Hypothermia is what happens when the leaks win. The NHS defines it as a dangerous drop in body temperature below 35°C,1 and calls it a medical emergency that needs hospital treatment. The cruel part is that it attacks the organ you need to notice it: the CDC warns that a cold brain leaves a person unable to think clearly or move well,2 so they may not realise what is happening.

The US Army survival manual describes the slide. Shivering comes first and can become uncontrollable as the core falls to about 35.5°C. Between 35 and 32°C come sluggish thinking, irrational reasoning and a false feeling of warmth.3 Below about 32°C the muscles stiffen and the person drifts towards unconsciousness. So watch each other: the CDC's warning signs in adults are shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness.

  1. Call for help. Call 999 in the UK, or your local emergency number, as soon as you suspect hypothermia.
  2. Get out of the wind and wet. Move the person indoors or somewhere sheltered as quickly as possible.4
  3. Swap wet for dry. Remove wet clothing and wrap them in a blanket, sleeping bag or dry towel, with the head covered.
  4. Get them off the ground. Slide a mat, rucksack or thick layer of dry leaves underneath.
  5. Warm the middle first. The CDC advises warming the chest, neck, head and groin, including skin-to-skin contact under loose, dry layers.
  6. Fuel the furnace. Give a warm, non-alcoholic drink and something sugary, but only if they are fully awake.
  7. Stay with them and keep them talking until help arrives.
Safety Hypothermia is a medical emergency, so always call for help if you can. The NHS lists things that will not help and could make it worse: no hot bath, hot water bottle or heat lamp, no rubbing of arms, legs, feet or hands, and no alcohol. If a person is unresponsive, handle them gently, get emergency help and, as the CDC advises, start CPR even if they appear dead.5

concepts.title: Myth check: it has to be freezing
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth You can only get hypothermia when it is below freezing.
Reality The CDC says hypothermia can occur at cool temperatures, above 40°F (about 4°C), if a person becomes chilled from rain, sweat or submersion in cold water.1 Mild, wet and windy is the classic trap: water and moving air pull heat away far faster than still, dry air, and the manual notes that dampness decreases the insulation quality of clothing. Exhaustion makes it worse, because shivering produces heat but also causes fatigue, which in turn leads to a drop in body temperature.2
Myth A bitter wind chill can freeze your skin even when the thermometer is above zero.
Reality Wind makes you lose heat faster, but it cannot cool anything below the air temperature. The National Weather Service is explicit that the air temperature has to be below freezing for frostbite to develop on exposed skin,3 although you might still get hypothermia. A car radiator on a windy night will not drop below the actual air temperature either.

Wait, really? Cold has killed walkers on English hills in spring. In March 1964, 80 teams of three set off on the Four Inns Walk,4 a 65-kilometre (40-mile) challenge across the Peak District moors. The weather quickly turned to heavy snow and poor visibility, and three Rover Scouts lost their lives. They had become lost in a snowstorm, and they had to cross the swollen River Alport again and again;5 two of them were found two days later just 2.5 kilometres from safety at Alport Farm. The tragedy led to the founding of the Peak District Mountain Rescue Organisation,6 and two years later the British Medical Journal published L. G. Pugh's report on accidental hypothermia in walkers, climbers and campers.7

title: Choosing Your Spot
description: Reading wind, water and cold air, and the dangers above, below and upstream of camp
tryIt: On your next camping trip, walk the site before pitching and point out one place cold air would pool, one route water would take and one dead branch you would not sleep under.

concepts.title: How it works: air that slides downhill
concepts.contentHtml:
The light is going and you are bone tired. The flat, grassy hollow by the stream looks perfect: sheltered, soft and close to water. It is probably the worst place in sight.

Start with the air. On a clear, calm night the ground radiates heat to the open sky and the air touching it cools too. Cold air is denser than warm air, so it drains downhill like water and collects in the lowest ground. The Army survival manual puts it simply: low areas collect the heavy cold air at night and are therefore colder than the surrounding high ground.1 Meteorologists call the result a cold air pool. A study by the University of Leeds and the Met Office describes radiative cooling making cold air near the surface, which drains down and collects in the valley bottom,2 and finds that the pools are closely linked to clear skies and light winds.3

Water obeys the same slope, faster and harder. A flash flood, in the words of Zion National Park, is a sudden increase in the depth and speed of water in rivers, streams or washes due to heavy rain, and it is often caused by storms miles away.4 The sky above you can be clear while a canyon fills. In a flash flood the water level rises within minutes or even seconds,5 and a wall of water and debris 12 feet (3.7 metres) high or more can rush down a canyon.

Then there is wind, which drives convection, and gravity, which works on everything over your head. Wooded country usually gives the best shelter, the manual says, because it offers timber, fuel and protection from the wind, but trees also drop branches and whole trunks. A good site is a compromise: high enough to escape the cold pool and the flood, low and screened enough to dodge the wind, and clear of anything that can fall.

concepts.title: In the field: the five-minute site check
concepts.contentHtml:
Before you unpack anything, walk the ground and look in every direction. The Army manual's two basic requirements are that the site must contain material to make the shelter you need, and must be large enough and level enough for you to lie down comfortably. Then run the check.

  1. Look up. Scan for dead limbs, loose rocks and dead trees that could fall on your shelter. Colorado forest officials warn that dead or live trees can fall without warning, even when it is not windy.1
  2. Look down. Stay out of dry washes, stream beds and anywhere below the high-water mark. Grand Canyon's advice, if you must camp near a wash, is to camp as high as possible and check for signs of past high water, such as stains on rock walls and debris lines.2
  3. Look around. In mountains, avoid avalanche and rockslide areas; in foothills, avoid flash-flood ground.
  4. Feel the air. Pick a spot a little above the valley floor, out of the cold pool, and turn the back of a lean-to into the wind.
  5. Find water, not too close. Leave No Trace guidance used by the US National Park Service is to camp at least 200 feet (60 metres) from lakes and streams.3
  6. Check the ground. Look for snakes, ticks, scorpions and stinging ants. Thick, brushy low ground harbours more insects.
  7. Watch the sky. Building clouds or distant thunder can mean a flood on its way down from upstream.
Safety Check the forecast before you go. If you see signs of a flash flood (water suddenly turning muddy, floating debris, rising water or a growing roar upstream), Zion's rangers say not to waste time packing up: reach higher ground as quickly as possible.4 Six inches (15 cm) of floodwater can knock a person off their feet. In a thunderstorm, Grand Canyon's advice is to keep away from cliff edges, lone trees and metal objects,5 and not to shelter in caves or alcoves.

concepts.title: Myth check: the cosy hollow
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The valley floor is the sheltered, warm place to spend the night.
Reality On calm, clear nights it is often the coldest place around. Researchers from the University of Leeds and the Met Office measured temperatures in the Clun Valley in Shropshire from July 2009 to April 2010. On 45 per cent of nights the valley floor was at least 1°C colder than the surrounding hilltops,1 and on 12 per cent of nights the gap was more than 4°C. The two strongest cold pools, 9.0 and 9.6°C, came on snowy January nights2 when the valley fell to about -18°C, even though the hilltop site was only 160 metres higher.3
Myth A dry stream bed makes a perfect camp: flat, sandy and free of rocks.
Reality It is flat and sandy because water made it that way. Grand Canyon National Park's advice is blunt: never camp in a dry wash.4 Zion's rangers add that flash floods can still occur when they are not expected.5

Wait, really? Dead trees do not need a storm to fall. After the mountain pine beetle epidemic that began in 1996 swept more than 4 million acres of forest in Colorado, Wyoming and South Dakota, officials estimated that roughly 80 per cent of beetle-killed trees fall within ten years of dying.6 A Colorado State Forest Service forester said his crews had heard and seen trees come down on calm days, and he advised campers to set up far away from dead trees.7 Campers have a grim name for a dead branch hanging over a tent: a widowmaker.

title: Debris Huts and Lean-tos
description: Why the ground steals your heat, a debris hut a metre thick, and the quick lean-to
tryIt: Lie for five minutes on bare ground and then five minutes on a camping mat or a deep pile of dry leaves, and notice how fast your back and hips feel the cold on each.

concepts.title: How it works: the ground is a heat thief
concepts.contentHtml:
You have found a good site, the light is nearly gone and there is no tent. Before you think about a roof, think about the floor, because the ground is the biggest heat thief in the forest.

Air is a poor conductor of heat; soil, rock and wet leaf litter are far better ones, and they draw heat out of anything pressed against them. Your weight also squashes your clothes flat exactly where you touch the ground, and the Army manual notes that heat escapes more easily through crushed air pockets.1 It goes as far as to say that when at rest you lose as much as 80 per cent of your body heat to the ground. Treat that exact figure with caution, since the manual gives no source for it, but its instruction is sound: never sleep directly on the ground, and lay down pine boughs, grass or other insulating material to keep the ground from absorbing your body heat.

Good insulation is mostly still air. In a standard physics table, wool felt conducts heat only a little better than still air (0.04 against 0.024 watts per metre per kelvin), because it is mostly air held in tiny pockets. A deep heap of dry leaves or grass works the same way.

People worked this out very early. At Border Cave, on a cliff between eSwatini and KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa, a team led by Lyn Wadley found grass bedding laid down at least 200,000 years ago.2 The sheaves of broad-leafed grass sat on layers of ash, which Wadley suggests was a deliberate way to create a dirt-free, insulated base for the bedding and to repel crawling insects.3 At Ohalo II, a 23,000-year-old camp on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, archaeologists found a brush hut whose floor was covered with grass bedding arranged around a central hearth.4

concepts.title: In the field: building a debris hut
concepts.contentHtml:
The Army manual rates the debris hut as one of the best shelters for warmth and ease of construction,1 and says that when shelter is essential to survival, this is the one to build. It is a long, narrow wedge, only just big enough for you, buried under a mountain of leaves.

  1. Raise a ridgepole. Rest one end of a long, sturdy pole on a tripod of two short stakes, a stump or a tree at about waist height, with the other end on the ground.
  2. Add the ribs. Prop large sticks along both sides of the ridgepole to make a wedge-shaped ribbing, wide enough for your body and steep enough to shed moisture.2
  3. Weave a lattice. Lay finer sticks and brush crosswise over the ribs so the insulation cannot fall through into the sleeping space.
  4. Pile on the debris. Heap light, dry, soft leaves, grass or pine needles over the frame until it is at least 1 metre thick, and thicker is better.3
  5. Stuff the bed. Put a 30-centimetre layer of insulation inside.4
  6. Make a door. Leave a pile of debris at the entrance that you can drag in after you.
  7. Weigh it down. Lay branches on top so a storm cannot blow the leaves away.

Short on time, with a fire going? Build a lean-to instead: tie a pole between two trees about 2 metres apart at waist to chest height,5 lean longer poles from it to the ground on the windward side, criss-cross them with saplings and shingle brush or grass on from the bottom up. Its back goes to the wind and its open face to the fire.

Safety Practise only where it is allowed: Leave No Trace guidance in US national parks says not to build structures,6 so in a park or on someone else's land, ask first. Use dead material from the ground, check the spot for snakes, ticks and stinging insects, and look up for dead limbs before you start. Dry leaves and pine needles are tinder, so keep any fire well away from a debris hut.

concepts.title: Myth check: roomy and roofed
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The bigger the shelter, the better.
Reality The Army manual says the most common error in making a shelter is to make it too large. Your body is the only heater, and every extra bit of air inside is air it has to warm. A shelter must be large enough to protect you, but small enough to contain your body heat, especially in cold climates.
Myth A good roof is what keeps you warm.
Reality A roof keeps off rain and wind, but on a cold night the floor matters at least as much. Even the manual's quick poncho lean-to comes with an instruction to reduce heat loss to the ground by putting leaves or pine needles inside. The American outdoor writer George Washington Sears (1821–1890),1 who wrote as "Nessmuk", made his overnight bed of hemlock browse a foot thick.2

Wait, really? The Ohalo II huts survived because they burned. Excavators found the remains of six brush huts that had apparently burned down in antiquity.3 Their floors were 2 to 5 metres long and 5 to 13 square metres in area, each slightly sunken like a shallow bowl, and the charred walls included branches of tamarisk, willow and oak up to 5 centimetres thick.4 Lake water and sediment then sealed the site, protecting the grass of the beds for 23,000 years.

title: Houses Made of Snow
description: Why snow insulates, building a quinzhee with a cold sink, and what iglus really do
tryIt: After a deep snowfall, push a thermometer down through the snow to the ground, leave another on the surface, and compare the two readings after half an hour.

concepts.title: How it works: a blanket made of air
concepts.contentHtml:
The wind is howling across open snow at -20°C, there is not a tree for miles, and the only building material in the world is the white stuff under your boots. Good news: it is a remarkably good insulator.

Snow is mostly air. The US National Snow and Ice Data Center explains that so much air surrounds each tiny crystal that most of the total volume of a snow layer is air;1 new snow in the United States usually holds just 4 to 10 per cent water.2 Trapped among the crystals, that air cannot move, and the NSIDC compares snow to the insulation in the ceiling of a house: it slows the flow of heat from the warm ground to the cold air above.3 Squeeze the air out and the magic goes. In a physics table, solid ice conducts heat roughly 15 times better than dry snow.

That warm ground matters. In 1959 Robert Elsner of the Arctic Aeromedical Laboratory and William Pruitt cited measurements from the spruce forests of interior Alaska showing the ground under the snow at around -7 to -4°C (20 to 25°F), with as little as 30 centimetres of snow and air above as cold as -48°C. In their own trials near Fairbanks in the winter of 1955–56, the inside of a shelter made of piled snow stayed nearly constant at 15 to 20°F (about -9 to -7°C) while outside temperatures ranged from -12 to -40°F4 (-24 to -40°C).

Arctic peoples knew all this long before the thermometers arrived. Inuit families built domed houses of cut snow blocks, and in the 1990s still used them as temporary shelter while travelling.5 The Nunamiut of the Anaktuvuk Pass region of northern Alaska were familiar with piling loose snow and hollowing it out,6 and the Kutchin of north-western Canada used a similar emergency shelter. It goes by a name of Athabaskan origin:7 the quinzhee.

concepts.title: In the field: the quinzhee and the cold sink
concepts.contentHtml:
A quinzhee needs no special snow and no saw, just a shovel or your hands, and time. Elsner and Pruitt piled snow over a weather balloon, but found that a parachute over branches would do as well, or nothing at all: it simply takes more time and work to pile up and dig out a snow mound.1

  1. Pick the spot. Stay off avalanche and rockslide slopes, and well away from roads and snowplough banks.
  2. Pile and mix. Shovel snow into a rounded mound; one Canadian guide suggests about 1.5 to 2 metres (5 to 7 feet) high and 2 to 3 metres (6 to 10 feet) across. Shovelling mixes cold and warmer snow, which is what lets it harden.
  3. Let it sinter. Leave the pile undisturbed for at least an hour;2 Watersheds Canada suggests 1.5 to 2 hours.3
  4. Push in depth gauges. Poke sticks about 30 centimetres long into the mound all over. When you uncover a stick end from inside, stop digging there.
  5. Dig in low, then up. Tunnel in on the downhill side and hollow out the dome, keeping the roof arched and the walls and ceiling at least 30 centimetres thick.
  6. Build the platform high. Make the sleeping platform higher than the entrance.
  7. Vent and close. Poke a ventilation hole through the roof, block the doorway with a snow block or rucksack, and put a mat or boughs on the platform.

Why the high platform? Heavy cold air slumps into the low entrance and stays there, while warm air rises to the platform and the dome. Elsner and Pruitt called an entrance built lower than the floor a "cold trap", and said that it, or an adequate door, was essential.4

Safety Snow tunnels can collapse with little warning:5 never dig into snowbanks made by ploughs, and use a buddy system, with one person digging and one watching. Any flame inside makes carbon monoxide, which has no colour or smell, so keep the vent open and never fall asleep with a stove or lamp burning. You will get wet digging, so change into dry clothes before you sleep.

concepts.title: Myth check: what makes an iglu work
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth An igloo is a hemisphere, like half a football.
Reality Picture-book igloos are; real ones are not. Researchers from the University of Alberta who built traditional iglus at Resolute in the Canadian High Arctic point out that a hemisphere is structurally unstable, because its walls would tend to spread outward until they failed.1 A working iglu is closer to an inverted paraboloid or a catenoid, a shape related to the curve of a hanging chain, in which the compressive forces grow towards the base.2 The builders trimmed the first blocks to angle upwards at about 30 degrees, setting off a spiral of blocks that climbs to the top.
Myth Your body heat alone makes an igloo cosy.
Reality It helps, but it is nowhere near enough. At Resolute in February 1993, with the outside air between -28 and -41°C, almost every spot inside the iglus was warmer than outside even with no heat source at all.3 Yet the team calculated that the body heat of a family of four would supply only 8 to 14 per cent of the energy needed for comfortable temperatures.4 The rest came from kudliks, soapstone lamps burning seal oil: the smaller iglu needed the fat of one seal every 6.3 days.5

Wait, really? Even an empty iglu is heated from below. The unoccupied large iglu at Resolute sat 5°C above the outside air,6 warmed by heat rising from the ground beneath it. Light a lamp and the researchers say you can expect the inside to climb at least 20°C above the outside temperature.7

title: Surviving the Night
description: Dry layers and dead air, a fire reflector wall, and two myths about hats and whisky
tryIt: On your next camping trip, seal one set of dry clothes, socks and a hat in a bag used only for sleeping, and change into them just before bed.

concepts.title: How it works: dead air and dry layers
concepts.contentHtml:
Your shelter is built. Now comes the long part: twelve hours of darkness in which the temperature keeps dropping and you must stay warm without moving much. What keeps you alive now is the air trapped in what you are wearing.

Clothing does not make heat. It holds still air against you, and still air is a poor conductor. The Army manual sums up its cold-weather rules in the word COLD: keep clothing clean, avoid overheating, wear clothes loose and in layers, and keep clothing dry. Each rule protects the trapped air. Dirt and grease mat the fibres and fill the air pockets. Tight clothing squeezes out air and restricts blood flow.1 Several thin layers beat one thick one, because each layer adds dead-air space2 and lets you strip off before you sweat. And water is the enemy: as sweat evaporates your body cools, and if a down sleeping bag gets wet, it loses a lot of its insulation value.3

Europe's oldest surviving cold-weather outfit follows the same rules. Ötzi, the man found in an Alpine glacier in 1991, crossed the mountains more than 5,300 years ago4 in clothing made solely of leather, hide and braided grass.5 His shoes were built in layers: an inner mesh of linden bast held a padding of dry grass in place as insulation, inside a deerskin upper and a leather sole worn fur side in. Experiments with faithful copies show they keep the foot warm but let in moisture,6 so he probably had to replace the wet grass from time to time. Dry insulation, changed when it gets wet: the rule has not moved in five thousand years.

concepts.title: In the field: a warm night by a reflector
concepts.contentHtml:
The American outdoor writer "Nessmuk" was sure what every forest camp needed: a bright fire in front, with a lean-to or shed roof overhead to reflect the fire heat on the bedding below.1 The Army manual adds a second reflector on the far side of the flames.

  1. Dry out before bed. Hang damp clothes high inside the shelter, or tuck damp socks and mittens, unfolded, inside your clothes so body heat dries them.
  2. Change into your dry layer. Keep one set of dry clothes just for sleeping, and loosen anything tight.
  3. Insulate underneath. Mat, boughs, leaves or grass: as much below you as above.
  4. Close the door. Block the entrance with a rucksack or a pile of debris to keep the heat in and the wind out.
  5. Build a reflector wall. Across the fire from your lean-to, drive four stakes about 1.5 metres long into the ground, stack green logs between them in two rows, fill the gap between the rows with earth and bind the stake tops.2
  6. Load the fire for the night. Nessmuk stacked heavy back logs against two stakes leaning slightly back, the largest log at the bottom, so they would not tip forward.3
  7. Warm up inside. Have a warm, non-alcoholic drink before you settle, and keep a hat on.

The physics: a fire radiates heat in every direction, and most of it would vanish into the night. A wall of logs and earth behind the fire sends part of it back towards you, and the slanted roof catches more and directs it down onto your bed. The manual adds that a fire wall cuts down flying sparks and the amount of wind blowing into the fire.4

Safety Fire is the biggest night-time risk. Keep it small, leave a safe gap between the flames and your shelter, and never leave it unattended. Any flame in an enclosed space can make carbon monoxide, which the CDC calls an odourless, colourless gas that kills without warning; people who are asleep can die before they have symptoms.5 Ventilate, and never fall asleep with a stove or lamp burning.

concepts.title: Myth check: hats and hip flasks
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth You lose most of your body heat through your head.
Reality Even the US Army's 1992 survival manual repeats it, claiming you can lose 40 to 45 per cent of body heat from an unprotected head.1 When Rachel Vreeman and Aaron Carroll of the Indiana University School of Medicine examined the claim in the BMJ in 2008, they traced it to an old military study in which people wore arctic survival suits but no hats. The subjects lost the most heat through their heads only because it was the only bare part of their body.2 Had they worn only swimsuits, experts say, no more than 10 per cent would have gone through the head. Any uncovered part of the body loses heat:3 wear the hat, and the trousers too.
Myth A nip of whisky warms you up.
Reality It makes you feel warm while you get colder. Alcohol widens the blood vessels in your skin, sending warm blood from your core to the surface,4 where it loses heat faster, and it can stop you shivering properly. A BMJ review adds that alcohol compromises gluconeogenesis,5 the body's way of making new glucose, and so its heat production. The NHS is blunt: do not give someone with hypothermia alcohol to drink.6

Wait, really? Cold makes you need the toilet. The Army manual calls it cold diuresis: exposure to cold increases urine output7 and drains body fluids you must replace, and your need for water is as great in a cold environment as in a warm one. Its field test is memorable. If your urine turns the snow dark yellow, you are becoming dehydrated and need to drink.
